Text | S.Li

Editing | Er Mu, Fanyu Meng

My sincere apologies: I’ve been swamped lately, tangled up in one thing after another, and couldn’t keep the active noise cancellation (ANC) articles coming on schedule. I hope you’ll understand. I made a public vow to write this ANC series, and I’ll finish it if it kills me!

Right, back to business. Earlier articles covered the types of ANC and the basic principles of feedforward ANC (FF ANC). This one is mainly about how feedback ANC (FB ANC) works.

If you remember the block diagram of FF ANC, you’ll know that in non-adaptive FF ANC only the ref mic is used, to pick up the ambient noise for FF processing; the error mic isn’t used at all. In adaptive FF ANC, the error mic measures the residual noise, which is used to adjust the adaptive FF filter. In FB ANC, adaptive or not, only the error mic is ever used; the ref mic plays no part.

The basic principle of FB ANC is to cancel noise using the residual noise picked up by the error mic. Compared with FF ANC, the advantage of FB ANC is that the noise measured by the error mic does not depend on direction. The input signal to the whole noise-cancelling system is the noise measured at the error mic, whereas in FF ANC the input signal is the ambient noise measured by the ref mic.

The drawback is obvious: FB ANC is always one beat behind! Think of the whole cancellation process like this: at time n I hear a noise x(n), I process it to produce an anti-noise y(n), and finally the headphone plays y(n). But note that by the time y(n) is played, it is no longer time n but the next instant, n+1! And at n+1, the noise we hear is no longer x(n). So FB ANC is always one beat behind! And of course the signal processing time can’t be ignored either.

In FF ANC, if the time for the ambient noise to reach the ref mic plus the signal processing time is less than the time for it to reach the error mic, fairly perfect cancellation is possible. FB ANC, even with zero processing time, is always one beat late.

At this point you may be puzzled: if FB ANC is always one beat behind, how can it cancel anything?

The answer: it depends on luck! If the noise at time n is much the same as the noise at time n+1, FB ANC can cancel it effectively. So when is the noise at n much the same as at n+1?

That depends on two things. The first is the frequency of the noise itself. The lower the frequency, the more slowly the waveform changes over time. Conversely, a high-frequency waveform changes faster over time than a low-frequency one.

The second is the latency of the whole signal processing chain, which matters far more for FB ANC than for FF ANC. To take an extreme example: suppose the error mic measures the residual noise at time n, but the anti-noise it generates can only be played through the headphone 1000 years later. The result is obvious…

By then you’re long gone, never mind the noise.

To sum up these two points: the anti-noise generated at time n must be roughly 180° out of phase with the noise at time n+1. That places real demands on the hardware: a fast enough DSP, low enough ADC and DAC latency, and so on. Both points apply to FF ANC as well, of course, but they matter more for FB ANC, which is why I bring them up here.

As Figure 1 shows, I made some simple plots in MATLAB to illustrate how sensitive low- and high-frequency sounds are to latency. Each plot has two curves: blue is the noise and red is the anti-noise. From top to bottom, the first plot shows a 100 Hz noise with an anti-noise that has no delay, and the second a 5000 Hz noise with an anti-noise that has no delay. We can see that if the anti-noise is 180° out of phase with the noise, the noise is cancelled perfectly.

But reality is cruel, and signal processing latency is ANC’s eternal headache! In the third and fourth plots, I added a delay of 0.1 ms to the anti-noise to see what happens. Clearly, a low-frequency sound (100 Hz) can still be cancelled (third plot): the anti-noise and the noise are still roughly 180° apart. But for the 5000 Hz signal, the phase difference between anti-noise and noise has become very small. Add the two together and you get perfect active noise amplification!

Figure 1. The effect of latency on low- and high-frequency signals

Liebich [1] calculated the relationship between signal processor latency and the upper frequency limit of noise cancellation. In Figure 2, the x-axis is the input–output latency (mainly hardware latency, from the ADC, DAC and so on), and the y-axis is the highest frequency that can be cancelled. The diagonal lines in different colors show the maximum attenuation in decibels.

Figure 2. The upper frequency limit of noise cancellation as a function of latency and attenuation (0, 5, 10, 15, 20 dB), with examples of some ADCs and DACs [1].

This brings to mind an ANC joke: a plane is roaring and a child is crying. I switch on noise cancellation, and all that’s left in my world is the crying child. That’s because jet engine noise is low-frequency, while a child’s wailing is high-frequency!

Back to the subject. Let’s talk about computing the FB ANC filter. We’ll start with non-adaptive FB ANC, since the vast majority of noise-cancelling headphones on the market today use non-adaptive ANC.

Figure 3. Block diagram of non-adaptive feedback ANC

Figure 3 shows a typical FB ANC closed loop. The residual noise e(n) recorded by the error mic is filtered by WFB(z) to give y(n), which is then played through the headphone. The acoustic transfer function from the headphone loudspeaker to the error mic is G(z).

Suppose the noise measured at the error mic without ANC is d(n), and we want FB ANC to cancel it. The ratio of E(z) to D(z) then expresses the noise-cancelling performance of the whole FB ANC system. In control theory, this is called the sensitivity function:

S(z)=E(z)D(z)=11+WFB(z)G(z)

If we take the sensitivity function S(z) as our objective, it should be as small as possible, because the smaller S(z), the smaller E(z), meaning less residual noise. To make S(z) small, WBF(z) would have to be very, very large. But here’s the catch: G(z) keeps changing (it differs from person to person and changes with the position of the headphones). The uncertainty of the whole FB ANC system is determined by G(z), and it can be expressed by the complementary sensitivity, T(z) = 1 − S(z). In short, because G(z) is uncertain, WBF(z) cannot simply be made as large as you like.

There are many ways to obtain the optimal WFB(z). For example, you can design one from experience and then derive WFB(z) from the average of G(z). S(z) describes the noise-cancelling performance, which typically looks like Figure 4. At very low frequencies (say, 20 Hz), ANC is not very effective, because microphones measure less accurately at very low frequencies (owing to their self-noise and so on). Between 20 and 1000 Hz, an FB ANC system can cancel noise very well. At high frequencies, latency and the uncertainty of G(z) mean there is essentially no cancellation.

Figure 4. Typical noise-cancelling performance of FB ANC [2]

Another typical approach uses mixed-sensitivity control theory to compute WFB(z) from the frequency-dependent uncertainty of G(z). There is a concise, clear paper you can use as a reference (it’s genuinely well written) [2].

The most common approach, as far as I know, is still the same as for adaptive FF ANC: run an offline simulation with adaptive FB ANC, tuning the parameters with different G(z) to optimize WFB(z). I’ll explain this in the section on adaptive FB ANC below.

Now let’s look at adaptive FB ANC.

First, a quick recap of the adaptive FF ANC system based on the FxLMS algorithm (see the earlier article for details). Put simply, in adaptive FF ANC the ambient noise x(n) measured by the ref mic is the algorithm’s input, and e(n) measured by the error mic is a feedback signal. In FB ANC, however, there is no ambient noise measured by a ref mic.

So what now? There’s no input signal!

Then let’s synthesize one! Figure 5 shows the basic block diagram of adaptive FB ANC. The algorithm and equations are essentially the same as for FF ANC. The only difference is that the algorithm’s input has to be synthesized: we create a noise signal ourselves. The synthesis path is marked in red.

Figure 5. An adaptive FB ANC system based on FxLMS

The residual signal e(n) measured by the error mic can be expressed as the difference between the noise signal d(n) and the measured anti-noise y’(n). The measured anti-noise can in turn be expressed as the output y(n) of the FB filter W(z), filtered by G(z). Since the output of W(z) is known, and we can estimate the current G(z) with its average G’(z), we can estimate the noise signal (in the time domain):

xsyn(n)=e(n)+p(n)+y(n)*g′(n)

With this synthesized input signal, the remaining steps are exactly the same as for FF ANC.

This is an adaptive ANC process, and it can run in real time (online) or offline. Offline, we assume the noise d(n) in Figure 4 is white noise and run ANC to obtain the optimal W(z). As with FF ANC, a psychoacoustic module and the like can also be added to the FB ANC process.

I’ve rambled on at length, but one point bears repeating: FB ANC is a closed loop, and its robustness and stability are determined by the ever-changing G(z). If that variability is not taken into account (for example, if the calculation considers only the mean of G(z)), this negative feedback loop can easily turn into a positive feedback loop. The result? Think of singing karaoke and holding the microphone too close to the loudspeaker: that howl.

That is my modest take on FB ANC. If you have questions or think something is wrong, please let me know. In the next article, I’ll write about methods for measuring G(z) in real time.

About the author: S.Li

An acoustics PhD student who has been roaming Germany for years, working mainly on binaural audio, psychoacoustics and active noise control.

References

[1] S. Liebich, J. Fabry, P. Jax and P. Vary, Signal processing challenges for active noise cancellation headphones, in ITG-Fachtagung Sprachkommunikation, VDE. VDE Verlag GmbH, Oct. 2018.

[2] S. Liebich, P. Jax and P. Vary, Active Cancellation of the Occlusion Effect in Hearing Aids by Time Invariant Robust Feedback, Speech Communication; 12. ITG Symposium, pp. 1–5, 2016.
